papers.title: BNIP3/NIX-dependent mitophagy: molecular mechanisms and physiological roles.
papers.summary: This paper reviews how BNIP3 and NIX, two mitochondrial outer-membrane proteins, tag damaged or unwanted mitochondria for selective degradation through autophagy, a process called mitophagy. It explains the molecular steps involved, including how these proteins interact with autophagy machinery like LC3 to trigger mitochondrial clearance. The review also covers the physiological roles of this pathway in normal cell function and development, beyond just responding to stress or damage.
papers.why: Understanding the core molecular mechanisms of BNIP3/NIX-mediated mitophagy provides essential background for interpreting mitophagy dynamics in neurons, which is central to this PhD project's focus on neuronal quality control.

papers.title: Integrative multi-omics and machine learning analysis identifies candidate biomarkers associated with mitochondrial quality control in major depressive disorder.
papers.summary: This study combines multiple types of omics data (such as genomics, transcriptomics, or proteomics) with machine learning to find biomarkers linked to mitochondrial quality control in people with major depressive disorder. Mitochondrial quality control includes processes like mitophagy, which clears damaged mitochondria to keep cells healthy. The researchers likely identified specific genes or molecules that could help diagnose or understand the biology of depression through mitochondrial dysfunction.
papers.why: This paper connects mitophagy and mitochondrial quality control to a major neuropsychiatric disorder, offering potential biomarkers and machine learning approaches relevant to your work linking mitochondrial health to brain function.

papers.title: Intensity-dependent effects of interval training on brain mitophagy, metabolic signaling pathways, and neuroinflammation in a rat model of type 2 diabetes.
papers.summary: This study examines how interval training at different intensities affects brain mitophagy, metabolic signaling, and neuroinflammation in a rat model of type 2 diabetes. Researchers likely compared exercise intensities to see which best promotes mitochondrial clearance and reduces inflammatory markers in the brain. The findings could reveal how exercise dose influences brain mitochondrial quality control and metabolic health under diabetic conditions.
papers.why: This paper is relevant because it explores mitophagy regulation in the brain under metabolic stress, which connects to the project's core focus on mitophagy/autophagy mechanisms in neurons, even though it uses a whole-brain physiological model rather than spatial or interneuron-specific approaches.

papers.title: Dual-mode SOX2 regulation by miR-150 via mRNA suppression and autophagy controls stem cell fate.
papers.summary: This paper studies how a small RNA molecule called miR-150 controls the levels of SOX2, a protein important for stem cell identity. It shows that miR-150 acts through two different mechanisms: directly blocking the SOX2 messenger RNA and promoting the breakdown of SOX2 protein via autophagy. Together these dual actions help decide whether stem cells stay stem cells or start to differentiate.
papers.why: Although focused on stem cells rather than neurons, this paper offers a relevant molecular example of autophagy-mediated protein regulation controlling cell fate, which could inform how autophagy/mitophagy pathways might similarly regulate protein turnover and identity states in neurons or interneurons.

papers.title: Unraveling the regulatory mechanisms of tetrandrine in microglial phenotypic transition and neuronal autophagy for relieving diabetic neuropathic pain.
papers.summary: This study investigates how the natural compound tetrandrine affects diabetic neuropathic pain by influencing microglial activation states and autophagy processes in neurons. Microglia can shift between pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory phenotypes, and this transition appears to be linked to how well neurons can clear damaged components via autophagy. The researchers likely show that tetrandrine helps rebalance this microglia-neuron crosstalk, reducing pain signaling associated with diabetic nerve damage.
papers.why: While focused on peripheral pain rather than brain interneurons, the paper's mechanistic focus on neuronal autophagy regulation and its connection to glial signaling offers transferable insights into pathways relevant to mitophagy/autophagy dysregulation in neurons more broadly.

papers.title: POU2F1 promotes hypertensive cardiac fibrosis by regulating mitochondrial homeostasis through PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy.
papers.summary: This study investigates how a transcription factor called POU2F1 contributes to heart tissue scarring (fibrosis) caused by high blood pressure. The researchers found that POU2F1 affects mitochondrial health in heart cells by controlling a specific quality-control pathway called PINK1/Parkin-mediated mitophagy, which normally clears out damaged mitochondria. When this process is disrupted, it leads to mitochondrial dysfunction and promotes fibrosis in the hypertensive heart.
papers.why: While this paper focuses on cardiac tissue rather than neurons, it provides mechanistic insight into PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy regulation that could inform analogous investigations of mitophagy dysregulation in neuronal health and disease within the PhD project's scope.

papers.title: SREBF2 promotes mitophagy and protects against ferroptosis via Cav-1-regulated PINK1/Parkin signaling in ischemic heart failure.
papers.summary: This paper studies how a protein called SREBF2 helps heart cells survive after a heart attack. It works by boosting mitophagy, a process that clears out damaged mitochondria, and by preventing ferroptosis, a type of cell death caused by iron and lipid damage. The mechanism involves SREBF2 regulating Caveolin-1 (Cav-1), which in turn activates the PINK1/Parkin pathway that tags damaged mitochondria for removal.
papers.why: Although this is a cardiac disease study, it directly examines the PINK1/Parkin mitophagy pathway, a core mechanism relevant to understanding mitophagy regulation that could translate to neuronal contexts in the PhD project.

papers.title: PINK1-Parkin pathway-mediated mitophagy in sepsis: friend or foe?
papers.summary: This paper reviews how the PINK1-Parkin pathway, a key mechanism for clearing damaged mitochondria (mitophagy), behaves during sepsis. It discusses evidence that this pathway can either protect cells by removing dysfunctional mitochondria or contribute to harm depending on context, timing, and tissue type. The review weighs these dual roles to ask whether boosting or inhibiting this mitophagy pathway could be a useful therapeutic strategy in sepsis.
papers.why: Understanding the context-dependent, dual nature of PINK1-Parkin-mediated mitophagy offers conceptual insight relevant to interpreting mitophagy dynamics in neurons, even though this review focuses on sepsis rather than brain tissue.
